source.title: Simple and Scalable Strategies to Continually Pre-train Large Language Models
source.authors: Adam Ibrahim; Benjamin Th'erien; Kshitij Gupta; Mats L. Richter; Quentin Anthony; Eugene Belilovsky; Timothée Lesort; Irina Rish

record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out validation loss at 405M and 9.6B parameters, but does not fit or evaluate scaling-law equations. This is a limited conceptual test of the parameter-count trend.
record.gate_note: The study reports paired model-size comparisons for validation loss and average downstream accuracy. It does not fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or measure compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Scaling-law findings cited in related work are not the study's own results.
record.test_reason: This is a continual-pretraining study. Its 405M vs 10B comparison (Tables 4–5) checks whether its re-warming, re-decaying and replay recipe still matches full re-training at larger scale. It is not a test of scaling laws. The authors frame the loss drop with size as expected ('As expected, we observe…'). With only two sizes and no fit, the results cannot speak to power-law form, extrapolation, allocation or predictability. The two sizes also differ in learning rate (max LR 3e-4 for 405M vs 1.2e-4 for 10B) and in shape (24 vs 36 layers), so size is not the only variable.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LR re-warming and re-decaying plus replay lets continually pretrained models match full re-training on average loss and evaluation scores. This holds across weak (English→English) and strong (English→German) shifts at 405M, and for the weak shift at 10B. They also propose infinite LR schedules that avoid re-warming. The size comparison is reported as an expected side result, not a scaling-law claim.
record.recipe_differences: This is a continual-pretraining study, not a scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation study; its relevant size comparison uses two parameter counts and held-out validation loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with training configuration, including the training sequence and replay fraction; the loss scale comparison is presented across matched configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Without replay, the 10B model forgets less Pile loss than the 405M model (0.23 vs 0.27 nats). The forgetting reduction from 5% replay is similar at both sizes (0.19 vs 0.21).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger language models forget less of earlier pretraining data during continual pretraining.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on the union of Pile and SlimPajama beats single-dataset training on each dataset's loss at 10B but not at 405M (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefit from mixing pretraining datasets grows with model size.

record.problems: Only two model sizes are tested; the study states that it did not run experiments over multiple seeds. Validation-loss standard errors were computed but not reported beyond stating they were < 0.001. Downstream evaluation is reported as aggregates, and the authors note likely evaluation noise for some base-model comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted from the selected scale comparisons. The paper contains other loss comparisons about continual-pretraining schedules and replay, but those test continual-learning interventions rather than the claim's scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Power-law form, several orders of magnitude, and token or compute sweeps. Only two sizes with differing LR are compared.
All of it. The two sizes differ in shape and size together.
No power-law fits in the continual-pretraining or repeated-data regime.
Predictability. Only two-point aggregate accuracy comparisons are reported.

record.verdict_notes: I overrode the record's 'tests/T2' and its V1 and V6 labels. The 405M vs 10B comparison is a two-point scale check of the paper's continual-learning method, so it cannot bear on any version's specific content. It is also confounded: max LR is 1.2e-4 at 10B vs 3e-4 at 405M (Table 14), and the sizes have different depth and width. The rows are all relinked to none. Average-loss rows (r3, r6, r9, r12, r15) are derived means of other rows. The paper cites Kaplan et al. only to say schedule choice was wrongly found unimportant, which Hoffmann et al. corrected.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares only 405M and 9.6B parameters in its scale comparison; it does not establish a power-law form, cover several orders of magnitude, or independently sweep tokens or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run loss are evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trends are evaluated.
The study does not compare architecture depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study tests text language-model continual pre-training, not other modalities or the listed alternative training regimes as scaling-law tests.
The study reports aggregate downstream accuracy comparisons by model size, not fitted predictions of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not test scaling-law fitting choices, fitted exponents, or departures from a single power law.
